question: Last December, the European Environment Agency published a report noting, ‘It is very unlikely that the 2030 target [regarding the agricultural area under organic farming] will be met because of the large distance to the target.’ If the current rate of growth is maintained, the share of organic farming in 2030 will be at 15 %, falling short of EU ambitions.

Furthermore, in some countries, the agricultural area under organic farming decreased last year. In Lithuania, for example, it fell by 6 %. This decline is concerning because it takes two years for farmers to switch to organic farming. 1.
What measures is the Commission taking to expedite the development of organic farming, especially in countries where such areas are not increasing enough or are even shrinking?

Have any Member States informed the Commission in the last few years that they will achieve a lower percentage of land under organic farming than initially planned under the common agricultural policy? If so, which countries?
answer: 1. The Commission continues to implement fully the EU Action Plan for the Development of Organic Production (1), emphasising in the current market conditions, whenever and wherever it can, in particular the importance of supporting and developing further the market demand for organic products via consumer information and education, agricultural promotion and (green) public procurement.
The maintenance and further development of the demand for organic products is the best possible incentive for farmers to convert to or remain in organic farming. 2.

So far, Bulgaria and Lithuania are the Member States that have proposed amendments to their strategic plans for the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) 2023-2027 lowering their targets for Result Indicator 29 (share of the EU agricultural area receiving CAP support for organic farming).
So far, the Commission has not approved any proposed amendment lowering the targets as regards support for the conversion to or maintenance of organic farming.
